title: The mitotic and life cycle of cells. Cell proliferation. Meiotic division of the cell. Pathology of mitosis and meiosis

goals.text: To teach the student the life cycle and mitotic cycle of the cell, the periods of interphase, the changes in chromosome set and DNA content in the phases of mitosis and meiosis, other forms of division, the types of asexual and sexual reproduction and the medical consequences of division errors.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the concepts of life cycle and mitotic cycle, the periods of interphase (G~1~, S, G~2~) and the checkpoints;
the groups of tissues according to the rate of cell renewal;
the phases of mitosis and the chromosome set (n) and DNA content (c) in them;
meiotic divisions I and II and the importance of crossing over and reduction;
the concepts of amitosis, endomitosis and polyteny;
the forms of asexual and sexual reproduction.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify the phases of mitosis on a slide of onion root tip;
write the genetic formula of the cell (n, c) for each phase;
explain the link between errors of meiosis and chromosomal diseases.

sections.title: 1. The life cycle and mitotic cycle of the cell

blocks.text: The **life cycle** is the period from the moment a cell appears by division until it divides itself or dies. It includes growth, differentiation, performance of a specialized function and aging. The **mitotic (cell) cycle** is the period of preparation for division (interphase) and of division (mitosis); it occurs only in dividing cells (Figure 3.1).

blocks.label: Figure 3.1
blocks.caption: Stages of the cell cycle: interphase (G~1~ — growth, S — DNA replication, G~2~ — preparation for division) and mitosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) followed by cytokinesis (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.title: Table 3.1. Periods of interphase
head: Period
Main processes
Genetic formula
rows: The cell grows; RNA, proteins and organelles are synthesized; enzymes for the S period accumulate
DNA replication, synthesis of histones; each chromosome becomes two-chromatid; centrioles duplicate
Tubulin for the spindle and ATP accumulate; DNA errors are checked
The cell leaves the cycle and performs a specialized function

blocks.text: Interphase may be **autosynthetic** (the cell prepares to divide) or **heterosynthetic** (the cell makes products for the organism and performs a specialized task). The cycle is controlled at **checkpoints** (G~1~/S, G~2~/M and the metaphase checkpoint) through cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases; if DNA is damaged, the **p53** protein stops the cycle or starts apoptosis.

blocks.title: Table 3.2. Groups of tissues according to the rate of cell renewal
head: Group
Feature
Examples
rows: Do not divide or divide very rarely after birth
Usually in G~0~; return to division after injury
Cells of the liver, kidney, salivary glands
Cells constantly die and are replaced from stem cells
Skin and intestinal epithelium, blood cells, spermatogenic epithelium

blocks.text: **Mitosis** (indirect division) is the main way somatic cells divide; it produces two daughter cells genetically identical to the mother cell. Mitosis consists of four phases and is followed by division of the cytoplasm — **cytokinesis**.

blocks.title: Table 3.3. Phases of mitosis
head: Phase
Processes
Genetic formula
rows: Chromosomes coil and become visible; the nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear; centrioles move to the poles, the spindle forms
Spindle fibers attach to the kinetochores, chromosomes move toward the equator
Chromosomes lie in the equatorial plane and form the **metaphase plate**; they are most condensed — the best time to study the karyotype
Centromeres divide, chromatids (daughter chromosomes) are pulled to opposite poles
Chromosomes uncoil at the poles, the nuclear envelope and nucleolus re-form; cytokinesis

blocks.label: Figure 3.2
blocks.caption: Formation of the spindle in metaphase: centrioles at the poles, astral rays and spindle fibers radiating from them, and chromosomes at the equator (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: In an animal cell cytokinesis proceeds by a **cleavage furrow** (contraction of an actin-myosin ring), and in a plant cell by formation of a **phragmoplast** and a cell plate in the middle of the cell. Higher plants have no centrioles, but a spindle still forms (without astral rays — “anastral” mitosis).

parts.text: Order of the phases: **“PMAT — Please Make A Team”**: chromosomes **P**ack (coil), **M**eet in the middle, **A**part they go, **T**wo nuclei form.

blocks.text: Biological and medical importance of mitosis

items: Ensures equal distribution of hereditary information to daughter cells and constancy of the karyotype;
Underlies growth of the organism and renewal and regeneration of tissues;
Is the cytological basis of asexual reproduction.
Failure of mitotic control leads to **tumors**; many anticancer drugs (colchicine, vincristine, taxanes) stop mitosis by acting on the spindle.

sections.title: 3. Other forms of division and pathology of mitosis

blocks.title: Table 3.4. Forms of division that differ from mitosis
head: Form
Essence
Where it occurs
rows: The nucleus divides by constriction, no chromosomes or spindle form; hereditary material is divided unequally
Aging and inflamed tissues, tumors, the macronucleus of ciliates
Chromosomes double without breakdown of the nuclear envelope, no cytokinesis — a **polyploid** cell
Chromatids replicate many times but do not separate — **giant (polytene) chromosomes**

blocks.text: **Pathology of mitosis** includes unequal separation of chromosomes to the poles (**nondisjunction**), tripolar or multipolar mitoses, lagging of chromosomes at the equator, and loss of the spindle under colchicine (**C-mitosis**). In somatic cells such errors cause **mosaicism** (two or more cell lines with different karyotypes in one organism) and **aneuploidy** in tumor cells.

parts.text: **Apoptosis** is programmed cell death: the cell shrinks, chromatin condenses and fragments, the cell breaks into apoptotic bodies and is phagocytosed without inflammation. It is important in embryogenesis (removal of the tissue between the fingers) and in eliminating damaged and tumor cells; its weakening leads to tumors and its excess to neurodegenerative diseases.

blocks.text: **Meiosis** is the division that occurs during maturation of sex cells (gametes) and halves the number of chromosomes. After a single DNA replication there are **two divisions** in a row (meiosis I and meiosis II), and four haploid (n) cells are formed from one diploid (2n) cell (Figure 3.3).

blocks.label: Figure 3.3
blocks.caption: Stages of meiotic division: meiosis I (prophase I, metaphase I, anaphase I, telophase I) and meiosis II (prophase II, metaphase II, anaphase II, telophase II) (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.title: Table 3.5. Stages of prophase I
head: Stage
Process
rows: Chromosomes appear as thin long threads
Chromosomes thicken; segments are exchanged between chromatids of homologous chromosomes — **crossing over**
Homologs begin to move apart, chiasmata (crossing points) become visible; human oocytes stop at this stage (dictyotene) for years
Chromosomes are maximally condensed, the nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear

items: **Metaphase I** — bivalents lie at the equator (the homologs of each pair face opposite poles) — 2n4c.

**Anaphase I** — not chromatids but **whole homologous chromosomes** (each with two chromatids) are pulled to the poles; the separation of each pair is independent of the other pairs — 1n2c at each pole.
**Telophase I** — two cells form in which the chromosome number is haploid but each chromosome has two chromatids (n2c).

blocks.text: **Interkinesis** is the short period between meiosis I and II; there is **no** DNA replication in it.

Meiosis II proceeds like mitosis: in metaphase II chromosomes lie at the equator, in anaphase II centromeres divide and chromatids move to the poles. As a result four haploid cells (1n1c) are formed. It differs from mitosis in that the chromosome number is haploid and there is no DNA synthesis before the division.

blocks.title: Table 3.6. Comparison of mitosis and meiosis
head: Feature
Mitosis
Meiosis
rows: Different from each other and from the mother cell
Constancy of chromosome number over generations, combinative variability

parts.text: Meiosis has **three sources** of genetic diversity: (1) crossing over; (2) independent assortment of homologous pairs in metaphase I — more than 2^23^ combinations in humans; (3) random fusion of gametes at fertilization. That is why brothers and sisters (except identical twins) are never completely alike.

**Nondisjunction** of chromosomes in meiosis produces disomic (n + 1) and nullisomic (n − 1) gametes. When they fuse with a normal gamete, **trisomy** (Down — 47,XX,+21; Klinefelter — 47,XXY) or **monosomy** (Shereshevsky-Turner — 45,X) develops. The risk of nondisjunction rises with maternal age because oocytes remain arrested in diplotene for many years.

blocks.text: **Asexual reproduction** involves one parent, takes place without gametes and is based on mitosis; the offspring is a genetic copy (**clone**) of the parent. In **sexual reproduction** gametes from two parents fuse; the genetic diversity of the offspring increases, which ensures adaptation to a changing environment.

blocks.title: Table 3.7. Forms of reproduction
head: Form
Types
Examples
rows: Simple binary fission, multiple fission (schizogony), budding, sporulation
Vegetative reproduction (fragmentation, budding), by spores, polyembryony
Hydra, tapeworm larval stage (echinococcus), identical twins
Conjugation (exchange of genetic information), copulation (fusion of gametes)
Fertilization with gametes; parthenogenesis (development from an unfertilized egg), hermaphroditism

skills.title: Skill: identifying the phases of mitosis in an onion root tip

items: Examine the permanent slide under low power and find the dividing (meristematic) zone of the root tip.
Switch to high power and find an interphase cell (intact nucleus, nucleolus).

Find cells in prophase (thread-like chromosomes, nuclear envelope disappearing), metaphase (chromosomes at the equator), anaphase (groups of chromosomes moving to two poles) and telophase (two nuclei, cell plate).
Draw each phase and write its genetic formula.
Count what proportion of the cells in the field is in interphase and calculate the mitotic index (cells in mitosis / total cells).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: The genetic material of a group of cells was studied and found to be 2n2c. After division, some cells had a DNA content of 2c and others 1c.
cases.ask: By what method did these cells divide?
cases.answer: Formation of 2c daughter cells is typical of mitosis: a 2n2c cell becomes 2n4c in the S period and after mitosis gives two 2n2c cells. Cells with 1c are formed after the second division of meiosis (1n1c). Thus some of the cells in the group divided by mitosis and others by meiosis (gametogenesis).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Under the action of a harmful factor, spindle fibers did not form in a cell.
cases.ask: Which processes are disturbed, and what is the result?
cases.answer: Without spindle fibers, chromosomes cannot gather on the metaphase plate and are not distributed to the poles in anaphase; mitosis stops in metaphase (C-mitosis). If the cell then re-forms the nuclear envelope, a polyploid (4n) cell with a doubled chromosome number appears. This principle is used with colchicine in karyotype analysis and to obtain polyploid plants, and with vincristine to treat tumors.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: Sex cells were found to contain more chromosomes than normal.
cases.ask: Which periods of meiosis may have been disturbed, and what is the consequence?
cases.answer: The cause is nondisjunction of a pair of homologous chromosomes in anaphase I (n + 1 and n − 1 gametes) or nondisjunction of sister chromatids in anaphase II. When a disomic (n + 1) gamete fuses with a normal gamete, trisomy (47 chromosomes) results: for pair 21 — Down syndrome, XXY — Klinefelter syndrome. A nullisomic gamete gives monosomy (45,X — Shereshevsky-Turner syndrome).

cards.back: Chromosomes at the equator; best for karyotype analysis
Centromeres divide, chromatids move to the poles
Doubling of chromosomes without cytokinesis → polyploidy
Pairing of homologous chromosomes in zygotene
Exchange of segments between homologous chromatids in pachytene
Failure of chromosomes to separate → trisomies and monosomies

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Mitosis — **one division, two identical diploid cells**; meiosis — **two divisions, four different haploid cells**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Stages of prophase I: **“Lazy Zebras Pace Down Daily”** — Leptotene, Zygotene (pairing), Pachytene (crossing over), Diplotene, Diakinesis.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Nondisjunction in meiosis is the main cause of trisomies and monosomies (Down, Klinefelter, Turner); failure of mitotic control leads to tumors.
